316.title: Human dignity (CCC 1700, 1929–1933)
316.hook: every person's dignity comes from God, not from usefulness
316.howItsDone: Human dignity is the foundation of Catholic social teaching; parishes and Catholic charities apply it in care for the poor, the sick, the unborn, the elderly, migrants and prisoners, and Catholics keep a feast of St. Lawrence each August.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Decalogue: ten words on two tablets. Your line was two tablets, one love. Today, why the second tablet matters: the worth of the neighbor.

Rome, in a time of persecution. A Roman official hears that the Church has treasure. He summons Lawrence, the deacon who looks after the Church's money, and demands it. Lawrence promises to show him. The story, as Ambrose tells it, is that the next day Lawrence came back with a crowd: the poor the Church fed. Asked where the treasure was, he pointed at them. These, he said, are the treasures of the Church. The official was not amused, and Lawrence was martyred. Catholics still tell the story on his feast day.
screen: `ROME: HAND OVER THE TREASURE.` → `LAWRENCE BRINGS A CROWD.` → `THESE ARE THE TREASURES.`

segments.voice: The Catechism opens its whole teaching on the moral life here: the dignity of the human person is rooted in being created in the image and likeness of God. Remember imago Dei, earlier on the path? This is where it leads. Dignity isn't earned, voted on or measured. It's given, by God, to everyone. If dignity came from usefulness, the productive, the healthy, the clever and the rich would be worth more. The letter of James pictures a man with a gold ring getting a good seat in the assembly while a poor man in shabby clothes is told to stand over there, or sit on the floor, and calls it judging with unjust thoughts. Worth, the Church says, doesn't come from what you can do. The newborn, the person with dementia, the unborn, the prisoner, the migrant, the dying: none of them has less. The Catechism asks everyone to look on the neighbor, without exception, as another self, and to take their life, and what they need to live it with dignity, into account. Social justice, it says, can only be built by respecting that dignity. And the respect reaches those who think or act differently from us. The Catechism quotes Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you." Dignity doesn't switch off when someone becomes hard to like. Lawrence knew the Church's treasure wasn't in a vault. It was walking around, hungry, in the streets of Rome.
screen: `ROOTED IN GOD'S IMAGE.` · `NOT FROM USEFULNESS.` · `THE NEIGHBOR AS ANOTHER SELF.` · `EVEN ENEMIES.` · then, large: `THESE ARE THE TREASURES OF THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Think of someone the world tends to overlook: a janitor, an elderly neighbor, a relative who repeats themselves, someone on the street you walk past. Picture their face as Lawrence would have seen it, a treasure, and then one small act of respect you could show them: looking them in the eye, asking how they are and waiting for the answer, listening a little longer. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Human dignity. The worth of every person, which Catholics say comes from being made in God's image, not from being useful. Today's word.
Your line: dignity is given. The treasure is still walking the streets. See you tomorrow.

317.title: The works of mercy (CCC 2447)
317.hook: seven corporal and seven spiritual works
317.howItsDone: Catholic children often learn the seven corporal and seven spiritual works of mercy by heart, and parishes organize them through food pantries, hospital and prison visits, funeral ministries and prayer for the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, human dignity: worth given by God, not earned by usefulness. Your line was dignity is given. Today, what that respect looks like when it rolls up its sleeves.

Jesus tells a story about the end of time. All the nations are gathered, and the king separates them, like a shepherd separating sheep from goats. To one side he says: come, you're blessed. I was hungry and you fed me. I was in prison and you came to see me. They're baffled. When? We never saw you hungry. We never visited you in prison. And the king answers with one of the most quoted sentences in the Gospels. The Catholic Church took that story and turned it into two lists, seven and seven, that children still learn by heart.
screen: `SHEEP AND GOATS.` → `WHEN DID WE SEE YOU HUNGRY?` → `TWO LISTS, SEVEN AND SEVEN.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims the king says: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Catholics hear this as Christ hiding in the people who need something. The first list is the corporal works, for the body. Six come straight from this story: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned. The seventh, bury the dead, comes from the book of Tobit, where a man risks his life to bury his people's dead. The second list is the spiritual works, for the soul. Instruct the ignorant. Counsel the doubtful. Admonish sinners, gently. Bear wrongs patiently. Forgive offenses willingly. Comfort the afflicted. Pray for the living and the dead. They're ordinary. Teaching a kid to read counts. Sitting with a friend who's lost faith counts. Not forwarding the angry text counts. And the word: in Latin, mercy is misericordia, from miser, wretched, and cor, heart, a heart that goes out to someone in misery. The Catechism calls the works of mercy acts of charity by which we help our neighbor in their bodily and spiritual needs, and says giving to the poor is one of the chief witnesses to love. Fourteen in all, and you don't have to do them all today. Feed, teach, forgive: three of them fit in a single afternoon.
screen: `YOU DID IT TO ME.` · `SEVEN FOR THE BODY.` · `SEVEN FOR THE SOUL.` · `MISERICORDIA: A HEART FOR MISERY.` · then, large: `FEED, TEACH, FORGIVE.`

segments.voice: Run through the fourteen slowly: feed, give drink, clothe, shelter, visit the sick, visit the prisoner, bury the dead; teach, counsel, correct gently, bear wrongs, forgive, comfort, pray. One of them has a face attached, someone in your life right now, so stay with that face and picture the work in something small enough to actually do. If you pray, you can pray for that person.

318.title: The body of Christ (CCC 787–796)
318.hook: the Church is one body with many members
318.howItsDone: At communion the minister says the body of Christ and each person answers amen, and in the prayers of the faithful at Mass the parish prays together for its members, especially the sick and those who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, misericordia: fourteen works of mercy, for body and soul. Your line was feed, teach, forgive. Today, why Catholics say doing it to the least is doing it to Christ.

A road outside Damascus. A man named Saul is on his way to arrest followers of Jesus, letters of authority in his bag. A light from heaven flashes around him, he falls to the ground, and a voice asks: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Not why do you persecute my followers. Not my friends. Me. Saul becomes Paul, and one picture he reaches for, to explain that voice, is your own body.
screen: `THE ROAD TO DAMASCUS.` → `WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?` → `NOT MY FOLLOWERS. ME.`

segments.voice: Paul's picture, in the Douay-Rheims: "For as the body is one, and hath many members; and all the members of the body, whereas they are many, yet are one body, so also is Christ." Then he says it straight: you are the body of Christ, and each of you a member. He imagines body parts arguing. The foot says, since I'm not a hand, I'm not part of the body. The eye would like to tell the hand, I don't need your help. Neither, Paul says, can be true. Then he flips the usual ranking: the parts that seem weaker are the ones that are necessary. "And if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it; or if one member glory, all the members rejoice with it." Stub your toe and your whole body winces. That's what Paul says a church is meant to feel like. The Catechism teaches that Christ is the head of this body, and that the Spirit gives the members different gifts for the good of the whole. Catholics say body of Christ at two moments that turn out to be connected. When the priest holds up the host at communion and says the body of Christ, the person receiving says amen. Augustine told new Christians in his sermons that with that amen they're saying yes to what they themselves are: the body of Christ. Be what you see, he said, and receive what you are. So the stranger in the next pew, whose name you don't know, is part of the same body. That's what Saul heard on the road.
screen: `THE BODY IS ONE, WITH MANY MEMBERS.` · `THE WEAKER PARTS ARE NECESSARY.` · `ONE SUFFERS, ALL SUFFER.` · `RECEIVE WHAT YOU ARE.` · then, large: `YOU ARE THE BODY OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: If you go to church, picture the people you see every week but have never met: the older man in the back, the family that's always late, the woman who sits alone; if you don't, choose a stranger from your street, your office, your bus. Hold one of them in mind; you don't know their story, and they're part of the same body anyway. If you pray, you can pray for them.
Soma christou, Paul's Greek for the body of Christ: many members, one body, with Christ as its head. Today's word.
Your line: many members, one body. One member's sorrow or joy is everyone's news. Day three hundred eighteen, done.

319.title: One, holy, catholic, apostolic (CCC 811)
319.hook: the four marks in the Creed
319.howItsDone: Catholics profess the four marks every Sunday and on solemnities in the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, which is also said, with differences of understanding, by Orthodox and some Protestant churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body of Christ, soma christou: many members, one body, with Christ as head. Your line was many members, one body. Today, four words that describe that body, said every Sunday.

Every Sunday, in churches from Manila to Lagos to Chicago, a whole congregation stands and says the Creed. Near the end comes a line that's easy to rush: I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church. Four adjectives in a single breath. The words go back to a council of bishops at Constantinople, and Orthodox and some Protestant Christians say them too, each understanding them in their own way. Catholics call them the four marks: the signs by which the Church is recognized. Today, slowly, one word at a time.
screen: `MANILA, LAGOS, CHICAGO.` → `FOUR WORDS IN ONE BREATH.` → `A COUNCIL AT CONSTANTINOPLE.`

segments.voice: One. Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." The Catechism says the Church is one because its source is one God, its founder one Christ, its soul one Spirit. One doesn't mean identical. It means one faith, one set of sacraments, one line of shepherds, holding many languages and cultures together. Holy. People sometimes laugh at this one, and the Church admits why: it's full of sinners, and has been from the start. The Catechism says the Church is holy not because its members are, but because Christ made it his own and gives it the means of holiness. It also says, frankly, that the Church is at once holy and always in need of purification. Catholic. It's a Greek word, katholikos, from kath' holou: according to the whole. It means universal, and also whole, nothing missing. The Catechism quotes Ignatius of Antioch, a bishop who wrote, tradition says, on his way to martyrdom in Rome: where Christ Jesus is, there is the catholic Church. Apostolic. The Church is built on the apostles, keeps their teaching, and, Catholics say, is led by bishops who succeed them, in a line of laying on of hands going back to the beginning. So the four marks aren't four boasts. Catholics understand them as gifts from Christ and as tasks: to become more fully one, more holy, more truly whole, and more faithful to what the apostles handed on.
screen: `ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM.` · `HOLY, AND NEEDING PURIFICATION.` · `KATH' HOLOU: ACCORDING TO THE WHOLE.` · `BUILT ON THE APOSTLES.` · then, large: `ONE, HOLY, CATHOLIC, APOSTOLIC.`

segments.voice: Say the four words on four slow breaths out: one, thinking of everyone saying it with you around the world; holy, thinking of one person whose goodness you've seen up close; catholic, picturing the whole, every language, every century; apostolic, thinking of the people who handed faith down to you, or to someone you love. Four breaths, four words, repeated until the bell.
Katholikos, the Greek root of catholic: universal, and whole, nothing missing. One of the Church's four marks in the Creed. Today's word.
Your line: four marks. One, holy, catholic, apostolic: four words, said in one breath every Sunday. Until tomorrow.

320.title: Other Christians (CCC 838)
320.hook: Catholics recognize a real though imperfect communion with all the baptized
320.howItsDone: Catholics join other Christians each January 18–25 in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, and many parishes share services, Bible studies and charitable work with neighboring churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the marks of the Church, katholikos: one, holy, catholic, apostolic. Your line was four marks. Today, the hardest of the four to see: one, when Christians are divided.

Thanksgiving, and the turkey is late. The grandmother is Catholic. One son became a Baptist when he married. A granddaughter goes to a Greek Orthodox church with her husband. A cousin is Lutheran. Around one table, four ways of being Christian, and old quarrels between their churches that none of them started. Someone says grace, and there's a small pause while everyone decides whose words to use. What does the Catholic Church say about the people at the other end of that table? Its answer is written down, and it's warmer than some of the guests expect.
screen: `ONE TABLE, FOUR CHURCHES.` → `OLD QUARRELS NONE OF THEM STARTED.` → `WHAT DOES THE CHURCH SAY?`

segments.voice: It starts with a prayer. The night before he died, Jesus prayed for his followers, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." Every division among Christians, Catholics say, runs against that prayer. Ecumenism, from the Greek oikoumene, the whole inhabited world, is the work of Christians seeking the unity Jesus prayed for. The Catechism teaches that the Church is joined in many ways to all the baptized who bear the name of Christian, even when they don't share the full Catholic faith or unity with the pope. It calls this a real, though imperfect, communion. People born into other churches today, it says, can't be blamed for the old separations, and Catholics accept them with respect and affection as brothers and sisters. Many elements of holiness and truth are found outside the Catholic Church's visible structure, and the Spirit uses them. Other Christians describe the relationship in their own words, and Catholics don't speak for them. Then, what changed. In 1964 the Second Vatican Council issued a decree on ecumenism. In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople lifted the excommunications Rome and Constantinople had exchanged in 1054. Since then: joint statements, shared prayer, and, each January in many places, a Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. Unity isn't finished. The Catechism says the work of seeking it belongs to the whole Church, every member and not just the clergy.
screen: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · `OIKOUMENE: THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `REAL, THOUGH IMPERFECT, COMMUNION.` · `1054 LIFTED IN 1965.` · then, large: `THAT THEY MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Picture Christians you know from other churches, a Baptist neighbor, an Orthodox friend, a Pentecostal coworker, a Lutheran cousin, around one table, and if anything in you tightens, let it soften. If you pray, you can use Jesus's own words, that they all may be one, holding each face as you say them. If you don't, simply hold the table in your mind, full.
Ecumenism. From the Greek for the whole inhabited world: the work of Christians seeking the unity Jesus prayed for. Today's word.

321.title: Other religions (Nostra Aetate, 1965)
321.hook: the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions
321.howItsDone: Catholic dioceses run interreligious dialogue offices, parishes share service projects and study with neighboring synagogues, mosques and temples, and popes have met leaders of other religions, as at Assisi in 1986.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ecumenism: the search for unity among Christians. Your line was that they may be one. Today, a wider circle.

Athens, the first century. Paul walks through the city and sees altars everywhere, one with an inscription: to the unknown god. Invited to speak on the Areopagus, a hill where the city's thinkers gathered, he doesn't mock their altars. He starts from one of them and reaches for words they already know. "For in him we live, and move, and are," he says, and adds that some of their poets had said we are God's offspring. Nineteen centuries later, the Catholic Church wrote a short document about people of other religions, and it sounds a lot like Paul on that hill.
screen: `ATHENS: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` → `PAUL STARTS FROM THEIR ALTAR.` → `NINETEEN CENTURIES LATER.`

segments.voice: In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued a declaration named by its first Latin words: Nostra Aetate, in our age. Its central sentence: the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions. It speaks with sincere respect of their ways of living and acting and their teachings, which, it says, often reflect a ray of the truth that enlightens all people. It names Hindus and Buddhists and their searching, and speaks with esteem of Muslims, who worship the one God and honor Abraham, Jesus as a prophet, and Mary. The same document says the Church also keeps proclaiming Christ, and holds both together. A whole section is about the Jewish people. It speaks of the great spiritual heritage Christians share with them. It says that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time, or against Jews today. And it deplores hatred and antisemitism at any time and from any source. After centuries of that charge, those sentences were written down at a council. In 1986, Pope John Paul II invited leaders of many religions to Assisi to pray for peace, each in their own way, side by side. The Church asks Catholics to meet their neighbors of other faiths with respect, to learn, and to work together for the good. Nothing true is rejected: not because every belief is the same, but because truth, wherever it's found, is taken seriously.
screen: `NOSTRA AETATE: IN OUR AGE.` · `NOTHING TRUE AND HOLY REJECTED.` · `NO COLLECTIVE BLAME ON THE JEWS.` · `ASSISI, 1986: SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `NOTHING TRUE IS REJECTED.`

segments.voice: Here is a prayer Jews say every morning and evening, from Deuteronomy, to hear as a guest, not to pray as your own: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Let it sound in you slowly, and think of the people who will say it tonight before they sleep. If you know someone of another faith, think of them too, and of the words they pray, and hold them with respect.

322.title: The communion of saints (CCC 946–962)
322.hook: the living, the dead being purified, and the saints, one family
322.howItsDone: Catholics profess the communion of saints in the Apostles' Creed, ask the saints to pray for them, pray for the dead at every Mass, and keep All Saints on November 1 and All Souls on November 2.

segments.voice: Yesterday, other religions: the Church rejects nothing true and holy in them. Your line was nothing true is rejected. Today, a circle that crosses even death.

Walk into an old Catholic church and look up. On the walls, in the windows, painted on the ceiling: faces. Apostles, martyrs, a young nun from Normandy, a Polish priest, a mother, a beggar. Now look down at the pews: a retired nurse, a kid on a phone, a man who comes every day since his wife died. And somewhere, the Church says, his wife too. Catholics see the painted faces, the people in the pews and the dead they love as one gathering. There's a line in the Creed that says so.
screen: `FACES ON THE WALLS.` → `PEOPLE IN THE PEWS.` → `ONE GATHERING.`

segments.voice: The Apostles' Creed says: I believe in the Holy Ghost, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints. Catholics say it at the start of the rosary, and promise it again at every baptism. In Latin it's communio sanctorum, and sanctorum can mean holy people or holy things. The Catechism says both are true: a sharing in holy things, above all the Eucharist, the sacraments, the faith, and a sharing among holy people. That one family of God, it says, exists in three states at once. Some are pilgrims on earth. Some have died and are being purified. And some are in glory, seeing God. Death doesn't cut the family in three. It's one family in three rooms. The letter to the Hebrews pictures the living as runners in a race, with "so great a cloud of witnesses over our head": the faithful of the chapter before, who bore witness by their lives, now all around the runners. And Catholics believe love and prayer pass between the rooms in every direction. The saints in heaven pray for those on earth; that's why Catholics ask them for help, the way you'd ask a friend to pray for you. The living pray for the dead who are being purified. And the good done by any member, the Catechism says, helps all the others.
